limits.title: Continual Learning for Smart City: A Survey
limits.text: The main bottleneck is the lack of well-developed large unified models, and key technologies like large-scale pre-training have not been adapted to urban data structures.
limits.quote: We believe that the trend would be to develop large unified models for processing different types of urban data.

limits.title: Continual Learning for Smart City: A Survey
limits.text: lack of high-quality and large-scale urban multi-modal datasets
limits.quote: The first one is the lack of high-quality and large-scale urban multi-modal datasets.

limits.title: Continual Learning for Smart City: A Survey
limits.text: existing multi-modal models become insufficient, and performing only fine-tuning can hardly meet the actual needs
limits.quote: However, when it comes to some data modes unique to urban computing, such as traffic and weather data, existing multi-modal models become insufficient, and performing only fine-tuning can hardly meet the actual needs.

limits.title: Continual Learning for Smart City: A Survey
limits.text: there is a large room for developing multi-modal models with continual learning abilities in smart city environments
limits.quote: Some existing studies are limited to specific tasks and modes [ 154 , 150 , 156 ] , so there is a large room for developing multi-modal models with continual learning abilities in smart city environments.

limits.title: Continual Learning for Smart City: A Survey
limits.text: There is very little research on this regard

props.title: Towards Reasoning in Large Language Models: A Survey
props.text: Large language models such as GPT-3 have demonstrated remarkable few-shot performance across a variety of tasks through in-context learning.
props.quote: Large language models such as GPT-3 ( Brown et al., 2020 ) have demonstrated remarkable few-shot performance across a variety of tasks through in-context learning. These models can be prompted with a question and a few ⟨ \langle input, output \rangle \rangle exemplars to potentially solve a problem through “reasoning”, either implicitly or explicitly. However, research has shown that these models still fall short when it comes to tasks that require multiple steps of reasoning to solve ( Bommasani et al., 2021 ; Rae et al., 2021 ; Valmeekam et al., 2022 ) .

limits.title: A Survey on In-context Learning
limits.text: Overcoming strong prior bias and ensuring models give equal weight to all in-context information remain challenges.
limits.quote: Overcoming strong prior biases and ensuring the model gives equal weight to all contextual information remain challenges

limits.title: A Survey on In-context Learning
limits.text: Most analytical studies are limited to simple tasks and small models; extending to a wide range of tasks and large models may be the next step to consider.
limits.quote: most of them focused on simple tasks and small models. Extending analysis on extensive tasks and large models may be the next step to be considered.

limits.title: A Survey on In-context Learning
limits.text: Enhancing the scalability and efficiency of ICL to support more demonstration examples remains a major challenge.
limits.quote: enhancing the scalability and efficiency of ICL with more demonstrations remains a significant challenge.

limits.title: A Survey on In-context Learning
limits.text: The scarcity of high-quality demonstration examples in low-resource languages and tasks poses a challenge to the generalization ability of ICL.
limits.quote: This scarcity poses a challenge to the generalization ability of ICL

limits.title: A Survey on In-context Learning
limits.text: Increasing the number of demonstrations does not necessarily improve performance and can even be harmful; these performance degradations indicate the need for further investigation.

limits.title: A Survey on In-context Learning
limits.text: Corpus-level demonstration selection strategies are more important but remain underexplored.

limits.title: A Survey on In-context Learning
limits.text: How to efficiently find the optimal order or better approximate the optimal ranking is also a challenging problem.

limits.title: A Survey on In-context Learning
limits.text: Research on calibrating bias or reducing sensitivity through scoring strategies is limited.

limits.title: A Survey on In-context Learning

limits.title: A Survey of Deep Learning for Mathematical Reasoning
limits.text: Standard few-shot promptings have not yet proved sufficient to achieve high performance on challenging tasks such as mathematical reasoning.

props.title: Against The Achilles' Heel: A Survey on Red Teaming for Generative Models
props.text: Attack strategies are classified into four key areas: Completion Compliance, Instruction Indirection, Generalization Glide, and Model Manipulation.
props.quote: We classify attack strategies into four key areas: Completion Compliance , which arises from the pretraining stage and leverages the model’s text completion tendency through autoregressive generation; Instruction Indirection , using capabilities enabled by instruction tuning; Generalization Glide , reflecting the model’s capacity for generalization, including reasoning and multilingualism; and Model Manipulation , which indicates a customizable model achieved by directly changing parameters, activations, or configurations.

props.quote: Before model explanations, popular attacks are loss thresholding and likelihood ratio attack (LRT) ( Pawelczyk et al., 2023 ) . compares.title: Machine Learning for Detecting Data Exfiltration: A Review
compares.text: Filter methods are computationally fast, simple to implement, and classifier independent, but have low performance and require manual threshold setting.; Wrapper methods offer good performance for specific models and consider feature dependencies, but are classifier dependent and computationally expensive.; Embedded methods learn good features in parallel to decision boundary learning and are less expensive than wrappers, but require fine-grain understanding of classifier implementation and are computationally expensive than filters.; Dimension Reduction techniques are computationally fast, transform features to low dimension, and are classifier independent, but are not interpretable and require manual threshold setting.; Attention mechanisms decrease development time of DL methods, automatically learn relevant features without manual thresholds, and yield significant performance gain, but are not reliable.

props.quote: The simplest format of family member detection task is to identify specific words, e.g., ‘brother’, ‘son’, in text that refer to the relative of the patient. However, there are several constraints that make the task less straightforward. The first one is that non-blood relatives, e.g., ‘adopted siblings’, ‘partner’s sister’, are usually excluded in previous work as their information are not helpful to analyse heritage diseases that the patient may have ( 8 , 25 ) . The second constraint is that the possible surface forms of mentioned family member need to be normalized with the side of family.

props.text: Treats the model as a black-box requiring only input/output access without delving into internal workings.
props.quote: This approach treats the model as a black-box and requires only the input/output access of a model without delving into its internal workings. This approach is specifically useful when the operator has no access to the model weights, e.g., for products and services wrapping API-based models. However, in the context of the RTBF, it does not yield any real privacy, as the models still retain the to-be-forgotten knowledge.

However, retraining’s flexibility comes at the expense of high (sometimes prohibitive) computational cost.

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools
compares.text: semi-autoregressive Transformer (SAT) extends syntactically supervised transformer (synst): Akoury et al. moved a further step to propose SynST, which autoregressively predicts a chunked parse tree and then generates all words in one shot.
compares.quote: Akoury et al. [53] moved a further step to propose a syntactically supervised Transformer (SynST), which first autoregressively predicts a chunked parse tree and then generates all words in one shot conditioned on the predicted parse.

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools
compares.text: tagged-BT extends noised-BT: Tagged-BT appends a preceding tag to every synthetic source sentence to help distinguish synthetic from genuine data.
compares.quote: As a result, they proposed a simple method called tagged-BT, which appends a preceding tag (e.g., BT ) to every synthetic source sentence.

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools
compares.text: back-translation extends back-translation: Iterative back-translation makes the source-to-target and target-to-source models enhance each other iteratively.
compares.quote: Hoang et al. [76] found that the translation quality of the target-to-source model in BT matters and then proposed iterative back-translation, making the source-to-target and target-to-source to enhance each other iteratively.

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools
compares.text: masked pre-training language model (mlm) improves standard language modeling: MLM allows the model to make full use of context, addressing the unidirectional drawback of standard language modeling.
compares.quote: Devlin et al. [55] proposed a masked pre-training language model (MLM) objective, which allows the model to make full use of context at the price of losing the ability to generate sequences.

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools
compares.text: bart extends seq2seq: BART pre-trains a denoising sequence-to-sequence model and then finetunes it with an additional encoder.
compares.quote: BART [ 85 ] took various noising method to pre-train a denoising sequence-to-sequence model and then finetune the model with an additional encoder that replaces the word embeddings of the pre-trained encoder.

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools
compares.text: mBART extends bart: mBART is trained by applying BART to large-scale monolingual data across many languages.
compares.quote: Liu et al. [88] proposed mBART which is trained by applying BART to large-scale monolingual data across many languages.

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools
compares.text: Lample et al. [93] compares Artetxe et al. [94]: Lample et al. used a shared encoder and decoder, while Artetxe et al. adopted a shared encoder but two separate decoders.
compares.quote: While Lample et al. [93] used a shared encoder and a shared decoder, Artetxe et al. [94] adopt a shared encoder but two separate decoder approach.

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools
compares.text: Yang et al. [95] improves Lample et al. [93]: Yang et al. proposed leveraging two separate encoders with shared layers and two different GANs to address potential loss of language characteristics in shared architectures.
compares.quote: Yang et al. [95] conjectured that sharing of the encoder and decoder between two languages may lose their language characteristics. Therefore they proposed leveraging two separate encoders with some shared layers and using two different GANs to restrict the latent representations.

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools
compares.text: Artetxe et al. [96] compares unsupervised nmt: Artetxe et al. and Lample et al. found that an unsupervised statistical machine translation system with iterative back-translation can easily outperform the unsupervised NMT counterpart.
compares.quote: Artetxe et al. [96] and Lample et al. [97] found that an unsupervised statistical machine translation system with iterative back-translation can easily outperform the unsupervised NMT counterpart.

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools
compares.text: Lample et al. [97] combines unsupervised smt: Lample et al. found that combining unsupervised SMT and unsupervised NMT can reach better performances.
compares.quote: Lample et al. [97] summarized that initialization, language modeling, and iterative back-translation are three principles in fully unsupervised MT and they further found that combining unsupervised SMT and unsupervised NMT can reach better performances.

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools
compares.text: Ren et al. [98] improves unsupervised nmt: Ren et al. proposed using SMT as posterior regularizations to unsupervised NMT to mitigate noise accumulation in pseudo-data during iterative back-translation.
compares.quote: Ren et al. [98] suggested that the noises and errors existed in pseudo-data can be accumulated and hinder the improvements during iterative back-translations. Therefore, they proposed to use SMT which is less sensitive to noises as posterior regularizations to unsupervised NMT.

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools
compares.text: Sun et al. [99] improves unsupervised nmt: Sun et al. proposed utilizing UBWE agreement to enhance unsupervised NMT, which is usually initialized by unsupervised bilingual word embeddings.
compares.quote: As the unsupervised NMT is usually initialized by unsupervised bilingual word embeddings (UBWE), Sun et al. [99] proposed to utilize UBWE agreement to enhance unsupervised NMT.

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools
compares.text: Wu et al. [100] improves back-translation: Wu et al. proposed an extract-edit approach as an alternative to back-translation to alleviate the low quality of pseudo sentences predicted by weak unsupervised MT systems.
compares.quote: Wu et al. [100] considered that pseudo sentences predicted by weak unsupervised MT systems are usually of low quality. To alleviate this issue, they proposed an extract-edit approach, which is an alternative to back-translation.

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools
compares.text: Artetxe et al. [102] improves unsupervised smt: Artetxe et al. improved unsupervised SMT by exploiting subword information, developing a theoretically well-founded unsupervised tuning method, and incorporating a joint refinement procedure.
compares.quote: Artetxe et al. [102] improved unsupervised SMT by exploiting subword information, developing a theoretically well-founded unsupervised tuning method, and incorporating a joint refinement procedure.

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools
compares.text: extension to the model of chung et al. [104] extends extension to the model of chung et al. [104]: Passban et al. proposed an extension to the model of Chung et al. which works at the character level and boosts the decoder with target-side morphological information.
compares.quote: Passban et al. [107] proposed an extension to the model of Chung et al. [104] , which works at the character level and boosts the decoder with target-side morphological information.
compares.about: extension to the model of chung et al. [104]

compares.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review of Methods, Resources, and Tools

compares.quote: Mixup and its variants typically develop and apply a global mix scheme to all features. For instance, Mixup draws a mix ratio from a Beta distribution, and each feature in the created example is a linear combination of the corresponding features from two sampled training examples, encouraging the model to understand data globally . In contrast, Cutmix and its adaptations intercept partial features from one instance and paste them on another, aiming to improve the model’s localization ability.

compares.title: A Survey on Human-AI Teaming with Large Pre-Trained Models
compares.text: In the Human-Steers-AI pattern, humans steer AI through instructions, corrections, preferences, or evaluation, while AI incorporates human input and adjusts behavior; risks include biased or inconsistent feedback.; In the AI-Augments-Human pattern, humans make final decisions using AI as support, while AI suggests, summarizes, or retrieves information; risks include over-trust or missing uncertainty.; In Mixed-Initiative Collaboration, humans work with AI as co-designers or partners, while AI suggests ideas or critiques outputs; risks include unclear roles or authorship.; In Dynamic Delegation / Control Handoff, humans step in as experts when needed, while AI flags uncertainty or escalates risk; risks include late or frequent handoffs.; In Emerging Supervisory Orchestration, humans set goals and monitor progress, while AI plans and executes multi-step tasks; risks include silent error accumulation or opaque tool use.
compares.quote: 表头: Pattern | Human role | AI role | Good for | Risks | Safeguard | 行: Human-Steers-AI | Steers AI through instructions, corrections, preferences, or evaluation | Incorporates human input and adjusts its behavior accordingly | Run-time steering, adaptation, alignment, and auditing | Feedback may be biased, inconsistent, or too narrow | Use diverse feedback, train evaluators, define clear rubrics, and include adversarial checks | 行: AI-Augments-Human | Makes the final decision and uses AI as support | Suggests, summarizes, explains, drafts, or retrieves useful information | Healthcare, educatio
